activity.detail: MDN If-Match If-None-Match ETag matching rules status codes

message.content:
The `If-Match` header uses a strong comparison algorithm, meaning it only matches if the ETag values are identical byte-by-byte; weak ETags (with the `W/` prefix) never match [1]. In contrast, `If-None-Match` uses a weak comparison algorithm, which allows a match even if the ETag is weak [3]. 

A failed `If-Match` precondition results in the `412 Precondition Failed` status code [2]. 

For `GET` or `HEAD` methods, a matching `If-None-Match` produces a `304 Not Modified` status code [3].

queries: MDN If-Match If-None-Match ETag matching rules status codes

passages.heading: If-Match header
passages.text:
## 

          Baseline

        Widely available

      This feature is well established and works across many devices and browser versions. It’s been available across browsers since July 2015.

The HTTP **`If-Match`** request header makes a request conditional.
A server will return resources for `GET` and `HEAD` methods, or upload resource for `PUT` and other non-safe methods, only if the resource matches one of the `ETag` values in the `If-Match` request header.
If the conditional does not match, the `412 Precondition Failed` response is returned instead.

The comparison with the stored `ETag` uses the *strong comparison algorithm*, meaning two files are considered identical byte-by-byte.
If a listed `ETag` has the `W/` prefix indicating a weak entity tag, this comparison algorithm will never match it.

There are two common use cases:

passages.heading: If-Match header
passages.text:
- For `GET` and`HEAD` methods, used in combination with a`Range` header, it can guarantee that the new ranges requested
come from the same resource as the previous one.
- For other methods, and in particular for `PUT` ,`If-Match` can be used to prevent the lost update problem.
It can check if the modification of a resource that the user wants to upload will not override another change that has been done since the original resource was fetched.

| Header type | Request header |
|---|---|
| Forbidden request header | No |

passages.heading: Syntax
passages.text:
```
If-Match: <etag_value>
If-Match: <etag_value>, <etag_value>, …
```

passages.heading: 412 Precondition Failed
passages.text:
The HTTP **`412 Precondition Failed`** client error response status code indicates that access to the target resource was denied.
This happens with conditional requests on methods other than `GET` or `HEAD` when the condition defined by the `If-Unmodified-Since` or `If-Match` headers is not fulfilled.
In that case, the request (usually an upload or a modification of a resource) cannot be made and this error response is sent back.

passages.heading: Avoiding mid-air collisions
passages.text:
With the help of the `ETag` and the `If-Match` headers, you can prevent conflicts or mid-air collisions.
For example, when editing some wiki pages, content is hashed and put into an `ETag` in successful responses:

```
ETag: "33a64df551425fcc55e4d42a148795d9f25f89d4"
```
When saving changes to a wiki page (posting data), the `POST` request will contain the `If-Match` header containing the `ETag` values that the client stored from the last edit to check freshness of the resource on the server:

```
If-Match: "33a64df551425fcc55e4d42a148795d9f25f89d4"
```
If the hashes don't match, the document has been edited in-between and a `412 Precondition Failed` error is thrown.

passages.heading: Usage
passages.text:
The If-Match header enables conditional requests by comparing ETag values. A client includes this header to ensure the server processes the request only when the resource's current entity tag matches one of the listed values.

For safe methods like GET and HEAD, the If-Match header restricts the response to resources with a matching entity tag. This selects a specific representation rather than validating a cache (cache validation uses If-None-Match instead).

For state-changing methods like PUT and DELETE, the If-Match header prevents the lost update problem. When two clients fetch the same resource, modify their copies independently, and attempt to write back, the If-Match header ensures only the first write succeeds. The second write fails with 412 Precondition Failed because the ETag changed after the first write.

passages.heading: Example
passages.text:
A client sends a PUT request to update a resource. The If-Match header carries the ETag from the original GET response. The server applies the update only when the ETag still matches.

```
PUT /document/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.re
Content-Type: application/json
If-Match: "a1b2c3d4"
{"title": "Updated Document"}
```
When the resource has been modified by another client, the ETag no longer matches. The server responds with 412 Precondition Failed and rejects the update.

```
HTTP/1.1 412 Precondition Failed
Content-Type: application/json
ETag: "e5f6g7h8"
```
Multiple entity tags are listed as comma-separated values. The condition succeeds when any one of the listed values matches the resource's current ETag.

```
If-Match: "a1b2c3d4", "x9y8z7w6"
```
The wildcard form succeeds when the resource exists. This prevents a PUT from accidentally creating a new resource.

```
If-Match: *
```

passages.heading: Why If-Match fails in production
passages.text:
Strong comparison makes If-Match sensitive to any layer rewriting the ETag between the read and the write, and several common layers do.

Compression is the most frequent cause. Servers applying gzip or Brotli often rewrite or weaken the entity tag for the encoded representation, and a weak tag never satisfies If-Match. A client reading an uncompressed representation and writing back through a compressing proxy sends a tag the origin no longer recognizes, producing 412 Precondition Failed on a resource nobody else touched.

CDNs and reverse proxies introduce the same problem when they generate their own entity tags. Load balancing across origins generating tags independently produces a different value per node, so the failure appears intermittent and tracks whichever backend served the read.

          Baseline

        Widely available

      This feature is well established and works across many devices and browser versions. It’s been available across browsers since July 2015.

The HTTP **`If-Match`** request header makes a request conditional.
A server will return resources for `GET` and `HEAD` methods, or upload resource for `PUT` and other non-safe methods, only if the resource matches one of the `ETag` values in the `If-Match` request header.
If the conditional does not match, the `412 Precondition Failed` response is returned instead.

The comparison with the stored `ETag` uses the *strong comparison algorithm*, meaning two files are considered identical byte-by-byte.
If a listed `ETag` has the `W/` prefix indicating a weak entity tag, this comparison algorithm will never match it.

There are two common use cases:", "- For `GET` and`HEAD` methods, used in combination with a`Range` header, it can guarantee that the new ranges requested
come from the same resource as the previous one.
- For other methods, and in particular for `PUT` ,`If-Match` can be used to prevent the lost update problem.
It can check if the modification of a resource that the user wants to upload will not override another change that has been done since the original resource was fetched.

| Header type | Request header |
|---|---|
| Forbidden request header | No |", "```
If-Match: <etag_value>
If-Match: <etag_value>, <etag_value>, …
```"]}

messages.content:
<tool_result tool="read_page" untrusted="true">
{"url": "https://http.dev/if-match", "title": "If-Match", "date": "2022-06-18", "passages": ["The If-Match header enables conditional requests by comparing ETag values. A client includes this header to ensure the server processes the request only when the resource's current entity tag matches one of the listed values.

For safe methods like GET and HEAD, the If-Match header restricts the response to resources with a matching entity tag. This selects a specific representation rather than validating a cache (cache validation uses If-None-Match instead).

For state-changing methods like PUT and DELETE, the If-Match header prevents the lost update problem. When two clients fetch the same resource, modify their copies independently, and attempt to write back, the If-Match header ensures only the first write succeeds. The second write fails with 412 Precondition Failed because the ETag changed after the first write.", "A client sends a PUT request to update a resource. The If-Match header carries the ETag from the original GET response. The server applies the update only when the ETag still matches.

```
PUT /document/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.re
Content-Type: application/json
If-Match: "a1b2c3d4"
{"title": "Updated Document"}
```
When the resource has been modified by another client, the ETag no longer matches. The server responds with 412 Precondition Failed and rejects the update.

```
HTTP/1.1 412 Precondition Failed
Content-Type: application/json
ETag: "e5f6g7h8"
```
Multiple entity tags are listed as comma-separated values. The condition succeeds when any one of the listed values matches the resource's current ETag.

```
If-Match: "a1b2c3d4", "x9y8z7w6"
```
The wildcard form succeeds when the resource exists. This prevents a PUT from accidentally creating a new resource.

```
If-Match: *
```", "Strong comparison makes If-Match sensitive to any layer rewriting the ETag between the read and the write, and several common layers do.

Compression is the most frequent cause. Servers applying gzip or Brotli often rewrite or weaken the entity tag for the encoded representation, and a weak tag never satisfies If-Match. A client reading an uncompressed representation and writing back through a compressing proxy sends a tag the origin no longer recognizes, producing 412 Precondition Failed on a resource nobody else touched.

CDNs and reverse proxies introduce the same problem when they generate their own entity tags. Load balancing across origins generating tags independently produces a different value per node, so the failure appears intermittent and tracks whichever backend served the read."]}
</tool_result>

The second write fails with 412 Precondition Failed because the ETag changed after the first write.", "A client sends a PUT request to update a resource. A server will return resources for `GET` and `HEAD` methods, or upload resource for `PUT` and other non-safe methods, only if the resource matches one of the `ETag` values in the `If-Match` request header.
If the conditional does not match, the `412 Precondition Failed` response is returned instead.

The comparison with the stored `ETag` uses the *strong comparison algorithm*, meaning two files are considered identical byte-by-byte.
If a listed `ETag` has the `W/` prefix indicating a weak entity tag, this comparison algorithm will never match it.

There are two common use cases:

Section: If-Match header
- For `GET` and`HEAD` methods, used in combination with a`Range` header, it can guarantee that the new ranges requested
come from the same resource as the previous one.
- For other methods, and in particular for `PUT` ,`If-Match` can be used to prevent the lost update problem.
It can check if the modification of a resource that the user wants to upload will not override another change that has been done since the original resource was fetched.

| Header type | Request header |
|---|---|
| Forbidden request header | No |

Section: Syntax
```
If-Match: <etag_value>
If-Match: <etag_value>, <etag_value>, …
```
</source>
<source id="2" title="412 Precondition Failed" site="developer.mozilla.org" published="2026-06-22">
Citation label: [2]

Section: 412 Precondition Failed
The HTTP **`412 Precondition Failed`** client error response status code indicates that access to the target resource was denied.
This happens with conditional requests on methods other than `GET` or `HEAD` when the condition defined by the `If-Unmodified-Since` or `If-Match` headers is not fulfilled.
In that case, the request (usually an upload or a modification of a resource) cannot be made and this error response is sent back.

Section: Examples / Precondition failed
```
ETag: "33a64df551425fcc55e4d42a148795d9f25f89d4"
ETag: W/"0815"
```

Section: Avoiding mid-air collisions
With the help of the `ETag` and the `If-Match` headers, you can prevent conflicts or mid-air collisions.
For example, when editing some wiki pages, content is hashed and put into an `ETag` in successful responses:

```
ETag: "33a64df551425fcc55e4d42a148795d9f25f89d4"
```
When saving changes to a wiki page (posting data), the `POST` request will contain the `If-Match` header containing the `ETag` values that the client stored from the last edit to check freshness of the resource on the server:

```
If-Match: "33a64df551425fcc55e4d42a148795d9f25f89d4"
```
If the hashes don't match, the document has been edited in-between and a `412 Precondition Failed` error is thrown.
</source>
<source id="3" title="If-Match" site="http.dev" published="2022-06-18">
Citation label: [3]

Section: Usage
The If-Match header enables conditional requests by comparing ETag values. A client includes this header to ensure the server processes the request only when the resource's current entity tag matches one of the listed values.

For safe methods like GET and HEAD, the If-Match header restricts the response to resources with a matching entity tag. This selects a specific representation rather than validating a cache (cache validation uses If-None-Match instead).

For state-changing methods like PUT and DELETE, the If-Match header prevents the lost update problem. When two clients fetch the same resource, modify their copies independently, and attempt to write back, the If-Match header ensures only the first write succeeds. The second write fails with 412 Precondition Failed because the ETag changed after the first write.

Section: Example
A client sends a PUT request to update a resource. The If-Match header carries the ETag from the original GET response. The server applies the update only when the ETag still matches.

```
PUT /document/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.re
Content-Type: application/json
If-Match: "a1b2c3d4"
{"title": "Updated Document"}
```
When the resource has been modified by another client, the ETag no longer matches. The server responds with 412 Precondition Failed and rejects the update.

```
HTTP/1.1 412 Precondition Failed
Content-Type: application/json
ETag: "e5f6g7h8"
```
Multiple entity tags are listed as comma-separated values. The condition succeeds when any one of the listed values matches the resource's current ETag.

```
If-Match: "a1b2c3d4", "x9y8z7w6"
```
The wildcard form succeeds when the resource exists. This prevents a PUT from accidentally creating a new resource.

```
If-Match: *
```

Section: Why If-Match fails in production
Strong comparison makes If-Match sensitive to any layer rewriting the ETag between the read and the write, and several common layers do.

Compression is the most frequent cause. Servers applying gzip or Brotli often rewrite or weaken the entity tag for the encoded representation, and a weak tag never satisfies If-Match. A client reading an uncompressed representation and writing back through a compressing proxy sends a tag the origin no longer recognizes, producing 412 Precondition Failed on a resource nobody else touched.

CDNs and reverse proxies introduce the same problem when they generate their own entity tags. Load balancing across origins generating tags independently produces a different value per node, so the failure appears intermittent and tracks whichever backend served the read.
</source>
</search_results>

Using MDN’s If-Match and If-None-Match references, compare their ETag matching rules. What status follows a failed If-Match precondition, and what status does a matching If-None-Match produce for GET or HEAD?

Under Read Committed isolation, a SQL statement sees changes committed by other transactions after the statement begins, but within a single statement, the data is consistent and "frozen" [1]. In contrast, under Repeatable Read isolation, a transaction sees a consistent snapshot of the data throughout its duration and will not observe changes from concurrently committing transactions [1]. 

The two backup components needed for point-in-time recovery in PostgreSQL are a physical base backup and continuous WAL archiving [2][4][5].

sources.title: Transactions in PostgreSQL: READ COMMITTED vs. REPEATABLE READ

passages.text: One important aspect of transactions in PostgreSQL, and therefore in all other modern relational databases, is the ability to control when a row is visible to a user and when it is not. The ANSI SQL standard proposes 4 transaction isolation levels (READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE) to allow users to explicitly control the behavior of the database engine. Unfortunately, the existence of transaction isolation levels is still not as widely known as it should be. Therefore I decided to blog about this topic, to give more PostgreSQL users the chance to apply this very important, yet under-appreciated feature.

The two most commonly used transaction isolation levels are READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ. In PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED is the default isolation level and should be used for normal OLTP operations. In contrast to other systems, such as DB2 or Informix, PostgreSQL does not provide support for READ UNCOMMITTED, which I personally consider to be a thing of the past anyway.

In READ COMMITTED mode, every SQL statement will see changes which have already been committed (e.g. new rows added to the database) by some other transactions. In other words: If you run the same SELECT statement multiple times within the same transaction, you might see different results. This is something you have to consider when writing an application.

However, within a statement the data you see is constant – it does not change. A SELECT statement (or any other statement) will not see changes committed WHILE the statement is running. Within an SQL statement, data and time are basically “frozen”.

In the case of REPEATABLE READ the situation is quite different: A transaction running in REPEATABLE READ mode will never see the effects of transactions committing concurrently – it will keep seeing the same data and offer you a consistent snapshot throughout the entire transaction. If your goal is to do reporting or if you are running some kind of data warehousing workload, REPEATABLE READ is exactly what you need, because it provides consistency. All pages of your report will see exactly the same set of data. There is no need to worry about concurrent transactions.

sources.title: PostgreSQL Backups and Point-in-Time Recovery with pgBackRest

passages.text:
This article is part of a series on PostgreSQL WAL.

Part 1 - How PostgreSQL WAL Actually Works

Part 2 - How Debezium Uses PostgreSQL WAL for CDC

Part 3 - PostgreSQL Backups with pgBackRest and PITR

In the previous articles, we've explored how PostgreSQL records every change inside the database using **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)**.

We also saw how tools like Debezium can read WAL to stream database changes in real time.

But WAL has another very important role.

It enables **database backups and recovery**.

By combining a base backup with archived WAL segments, PostgreSQL can restore a database to **any specific moment in time**. This capability is known as **Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)**.

In this article, we’ll explore how this works and how to implement it using pgBackRest.

passages.heading: How WAL Enables Point-in-Time Recovery
passages.text:
Point-in-Time Recovery works by combining two components:

```
                              Base Backup
                                   +
                        Continuous WAL Archiving
                                   =
                         Point-in-Time Recovery
```
The recovery flow looks like this:

```
                               Base Backup
                                    │
                                    ▼
                              Restore Backup
                                    │
                                    ▼
                           Replay WAL Segments
                                    │
                                    ▼
                            Reach Target Time
```
Because WAL contains every change in chronological order, PostgreSQL can replay those changes to reconstruct the database state at any moment.

passages.heading: Final Thoughts
passages.text:
Throughout this series, we’ve seen how **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)** forms the foundation for several critical PostgreSQL features.

The same WAL mechanism powers:

- crash recovery
- replication
- change data capture
- backups
- point-in-time recovery

Understanding WAL makes it easier to understand how PostgreSQL maintains reliability and data safety in production environments.

Tools like pgBackRest build on top of this mechanism to provide robust backup and restore workflows.

inchirags@gmail.com Chirag's PostgreSQL DBA Tutorial https://www.chirags.in

*************************************************************************************

Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) guide using Physical Backup and WAL archiving in PostgreSQL 17 across two Windows Servers

*************************************************************************************

Here's the step-by-step Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) guide using Physical Backup and WAL archiving in PostgreSQL 17 across two Windows Servers. This is a conversion of your Linux-based guide tailored for Windows Server environment.

✅ Environment Setup

```
Role		IP Address	Description
-------------------------------------------------------------------------
Primary		192.168.224.133	Active PostgreSQL Server before crash
Recovery	192.168.224.134	Server used to perform PITR        
```

```

    PostgreSQL Service User: postgres
    Password: admin@123

    Data Directory: C:\PostgreSQL\data
    Backup Dir: C:\PostgreSQL\database_backup
    Archive Dir: C:\PostgreSQL\database_archive        
```

          🔧 Step-by-Step Guide

✅ Step 1: Install PostgreSQL 17 on Both Servers

Download from:

    `https://www.enterprisedb.com/downloads/postgres-postgresql-downloads`        

          Run the installer:

```
        Choose components: PostgreSQL Server + Command Line Tools
        Set password for postgres: admin@123
        Install to: C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL\17
        Data directory: C:\PostgreSQL\data        
```

          After install, ensure PostgreSQL service is running (services.msc > PostgreSQL 17)

✅ Step 2: Set postgres User Password

passages.heading: Recommended by LinkedIn
passages.text:
✅ Step 9: Give the full security permission for user in folder "C:\PostgreSQL\data" and Start PostgreSQL on Recovery Server

`net start postgresql-x64-17`        

          Check service status in services.msc or Event Viewer.

✅ Step 10: Verify Recovery Status

In SQL Shell (psql):

`\c chirags_db1`        

          `\dt`        

          `SELECT * FROM users;`        

          `SELECT * FROM accounts;`        

          If you see both users and accounts tables, PITR was successful.

✅ Step 11: Exit Read-Only Mode

`SELECT pg_wal_replay_resume();`        

          🎉 Final Output Validation

`SELECT * FROM users;`        

          `SELECT * FROM accounts;`        

          `SELECT now();`        

          ✅ Summary

Plenty of Kubernetes backup content treats point-in-time recovery like a fancy snapshot feature. That is not how PostgreSQL works.

PostgreSQL point-in-time recovery, or PITR, is a recovery model built from two things together:

- a physical base backup
- a continuous archive of write-ahead log, or WAL, files

The current PostgreSQL documentation is explicit about this. PITR combines a file-system-level backup with archived WAL, then replays WAL until the target time you want to restore to. In other words, snapshots can help, but snapshots alone are not PITR.

That distinction matters even more on Kubernetes, where teams often have:

- CSI snapshots
- operator-managed backups
- object-store retention
- multiple PVCs
- automation that looks reassuring until the first real restore

passages.heading: A Practical PITR Design for Kubernetes
passages.text:
If you want a design that is operationally sane, keep it simple:

- take regular physical base backups
- archive WAL continuously to object storage
- use snapshots to accelerate recovery when your storage stack supports them
- restore into a new cluster, then validate before promotion

That avoids two common traps:

- treating snapshots as the whole disaster-recovery plan
- overcomplicating recovery with too many one-off scripts and manual steps

If your operator supports it, snapshot-based recovery can shorten the time needed to rehydrate large datasets. CloudNativePG, for example, supports restoring from a `VolumeSnapshot` and then applying archived WAL to reach the target time. It also warns that if you use separate WAL storage, that snapshot must be included too.

passages.heading: What does PostgreSQL PITR on Kubernetes actually require?
passages.text: At minimum, you need a recoverable base backup, continuous WAL archiving, and a tested restore workflow that can recover to a specific target time or restore point.

sources.title: PostgreSQL Point-in-Time Recovery with WAL Archiving | Stack Harbor

passages.text: Point-in-time recovery (PITR) lets you restore a self-managed PostgreSQL cluster to any exact moment — the instant before a bad `DELETE`, not just last night’s snapshot. It rests on two pieces: a physical base backup taken with `pg_basebackup`, and a continuous stream of write-ahead log (WAL) segments shipped off the server by `archive_command`. To recover, you lay down the base backup, point `restore_command` at the WAL archive, set `recovery_target_time` to the moment you want, drop a `recovery.signal` file, and start the server. It replays WAL forward from the backup until it reaches your target, then stops. On PostgreSQL 15, 16, and 17 the old `recovery.conf` is gone — recovery settings live in `postgresql.auto.conf` and the presence of `recovery.signal` is what puts the server into recovery mode. The configuration is a few lines; the part that actually saves you is rehearsing the restore before you need it.

passages.heading: Step-by-step
passages.text:
```
LOG:  starting point-in-time recovery to 2026-07-21 14:19:55-04
LOG:  restored log file "000000010000000000000004" from archive
LOG:  recovery stopping before commit of transaction 1234, time 2026-07-21 14:19:56.02-04
LOG:  recovery has paused
HINT:  Execute pg_wal_replay_resume() to promote.
```
**10. Inspect, then promote.** Connect and check the data (see the next section). When satisfied, end recovery and open the cluster read-write.

`SELECT pg_wal_replay_resume();`
The server finishes on a new timeline and begins accepting writes. `pg_promote()` is the equivalent when you want to force the end immediately.

passages.heading: When this is the wrong approach
passages.text:
For the authoritative reference on every parameter, see the PostgreSQL manual on Continuous Archiving and Point-in-Time Recovery and the recovery target settings.

If this is the kind of work you’d rather never own again, it’s the daily job of Managed Cloud Ops — book an infrastructure review.

{"url": "https://cybertec-postgresql.com/en/transactions-in-postgresql-read-committed-vs-repeatable-read", "title": "Transactions in PostgreSQL: READ COMMITTED vs. REPEATABLE READ", "date": "2018-11-28", "passages": ["One important aspect of transactions in PostgreSQL, and therefore in all other modern relational databases, is the ability to control when a row is visible to a user and when it is not. The ANSI SQL standard proposes 4 transaction isolation levels (READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE) to allow users to explicitly control the behavior of the database engine. Unfortunately, the existence of transaction isolation levels is still not as widely known as it should be. Therefore I decided to blog about this topic, to give more PostgreSQL users the chance to apply this very important, yet under-appreciated feature.", "The two most commonly used transaction isolation levels are READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ. In PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED is the default isolation level and should be used for normal OLTP operations. In contrast to other systems, such as DB2 or Informix, PostgreSQL does not provide support for READ UNCOMMITTED, which I personally consider to be a thing of the past anyway.\n\nIn READ COMMITTED mode, every SQL statement will see changes which have already been committed (e.g. new rows added to the database) by some other transactions. In other words: If you run the same SELECT statement multiple times within the same transaction, you might see different results. This is something you have to consider when writing an application.", "However, within a statement the data you see is constant – it does not change. A SELECT statement (or any other statement) will not see changes committed WHILE the statement is running. Within an SQL statement, data and time are basically “frozen”.\n\nIn the case of REPEATABLE READ the situation is quite different: A transaction running in REPEATABLE READ mode will never see the effects of transactions committing concurrently – it will keep seeing the same data and offer you a consistent snapshot throughout the entire transaction. If your goal is to do reporting or if you are running some kind of data warehousing workload, REPEATABLE READ is exactly what you need, because it provides consistency. All pages of your report will see exactly the same set of data. There is no need to worry about concurrent transactions."]}
</tool_result>

The ANSI SQL standard proposes 4 transaction isolation levels (READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE) to allow users to explicitly control the behavior of the database engine. Unfortunately, the existence of transaction isolation levels is still not as widely known as it should be. Therefore I decided to blog about this topic, to give more PostgreSQL users the chance to apply this very important, yet under-appreciated feature.", "The two most commonly used transaction isolation levels are READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ. In PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED is the default isolation level and should be used for normal OLTP operations. In contrast to other systems, such as DB2 or Informix, PostgreSQL does not provide support for READ UNCOMMITTED, which I personally consider to be a thing of the past anyway.\n\nIn READ COMMITTED mode, every SQL statement will see changes which have already been committed (e.g. new rows added to the database) by some other transactions. In other words: If you run the same SELECT statement multiple times within the same transaction, you might see different results. This is something you have to consider when writing an application.", "However, within a statement the data you see is constant – it does not change. A SELECT statement (or any other statement) will not see changes committed WHILE the statement is running. Within an SQL statement, data and time are basically “frozen”.\n\nIn the case of REPEATABLE READ the situation is quite different: A transaction running in REPEATABLE READ mode will never see the effects of transactions committing concurrently – it will keep seeing the same data and offer you a consistent snapshot throughout the entire transaction. If your goal is to do reporting or if you are running some kind of data warehousing workload, REPEATABLE READ is exactly what you need, because it provides consistency. All pages of your report will see exactly the same set of data. There is no need to worry about concurrent transactions."]}

Part 1 - How PostgreSQL WAL Actually Works

Part 2 - How Debezium Uses PostgreSQL WAL for CDC

Part 3 - PostgreSQL Backups with pgBackRest and PITR

In the previous articles, we've explored how PostgreSQL records every change inside the database using **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)**.

We also saw how tools like Debezium can read WAL to stream database changes in real time.

But WAL has another very important role.

It enables **database backups and recovery**.

By combining a base backup with archived WAL segments, PostgreSQL can restore a database to **any specific moment in time**. This capability is known as **Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)**.

In this article, we’ll explore how this works and how to implement it using pgBackRest.", "Point-in-Time Recovery works by combining two components:

```
                              Base Backup
                                   +
                        Continuous WAL Archiving
                                   =
                         Point-in-Time Recovery
```
The recovery flow looks like this:

```
                               Base Backup
                                    │
                                    ▼
                              Restore Backup
                                    │
                                    ▼
                           Replay WAL Segments
                                    │
                                    ▼
                            Reach Target Time
```
Because WAL contains every change in chronological order, PostgreSQL can replay those changes to reconstruct the database state at any moment.", "Throughout this series, we’ve seen how **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)** forms the foundation for several critical PostgreSQL features.

The same WAL mechanism powers:

- crash recovery
- replication
- change data capture
- backups
- point-in-time recovery

Understanding WAL makes it easier to understand how PostgreSQL maintains reliability and data safety in production environments.

Tools like pgBackRest build on top of this mechanism to provide robust backup and restore workflows."]}

{"url": "https://cybertec-postgresql.com/en/transactions-in-postgresql-read-committed-vs-repeatable-read", "title": "Transactions in PostgreSQL: READ COMMITTED vs. REPEATABLE READ", "date": "2018-11-28", "passages": ["One important aspect of transactions in PostgreSQL, and therefore in all other modern relational databases, is the ability to control when a row is visible to a user and when it is not. The ANSI SQL standard proposes 4 transaction isolation levels (READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE) to allow users to explicitly control the behavior of the database engine. Unfortunately, the existence of transaction isolation levels is still not as widely known as it should be. Therefore I decided to blog about this topic, to give more PostgreSQL users the chance to apply this very important, yet under-appreciated feature.", "The two most commonly used transaction isolation levels are READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ. In PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED is the default isolation level and should be used for normal OLTP operations. In contrast to other systems, such as DB2 or Informix, PostgreSQL does not provide support for READ UNCOMMITTED, which I personally consider to be a thing of the past anyway.\n\nIn READ COMMITTED mode, every SQL statement will see changes which have already been committed (e.g. new rows added to the database) by some other transactions. In other words: If you run the same SELECT statement multiple times within the same transaction, you might see different results. This is something you have to consider when writing an application.", "However, within a statement the data you see is constant – it does not change. A SELECT statement (or any other statement) will not see changes committed WHILE the statement is running. Within an SQL statement, data and time are basically “frozen”.\n\nIn the case of REPEATABLE READ the situation is quite different: A transaction running in REPEATABLE READ mode will never see the effects of transactions committing concurrently – it will keep seeing the same data and offer you a consistent snapshot throughout the entire transaction. If your goal is to do reporting or if you are running some kind of data warehousing workload, REPEATABLE READ is exactly what you need, because it provides consistency. All pages of your report will see exactly the same set of data. There is no need to worry about concurrent transactions."]}
</tool_result>

Part 1 - How PostgreSQL WAL Actually Works

Part 2 - How Debezium Uses PostgreSQL WAL for CDC

Part 3 - PostgreSQL Backups with pgBackRest and PITR

In the previous articles, we've explored how PostgreSQL records every change inside the database using **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)**.

We also saw how tools like Debezium can read WAL to stream database changes in real time.

But WAL has another very important role.

It enables **database backups and recovery**.

By combining a base backup with archived WAL segments, PostgreSQL can restore a database to **any specific moment in time**. This capability is known as **Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)**.

In this article, we’ll explore how this works and how to implement it using pgBackRest.", "Point-in-Time Recovery works by combining two components:

```
                              Base Backup
                                   +
                        Continuous WAL Archiving
                                   =
                         Point-in-Time Recovery
```
The recovery flow looks like this:

```
                               Base Backup
                                    │
                                    ▼
                              Restore Backup
                                    │
                                    ▼
                           Replay WAL Segments
                                    │
                                    ▼
                            Reach Target Time
```
Because WAL contains every change in chronological order, PostgreSQL can replay those changes to reconstruct the database state at any moment.", "Throughout this series, we’ve seen how **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)** forms the foundation for several critical PostgreSQL features.

The same WAL mechanism powers:

- crash recovery
- replication
- change data capture
- backups
- point-in-time recovery

Understanding WAL makes it easier to understand how PostgreSQL maintains reliability and data safety in production environments.

Tools like pgBackRest build on top of this mechanism to provide robust backup and restore workflows."]}
</tool_result>

{"url": "https://cybertec-postgresql.com/en/transactions-in-postgresql-read-committed-vs-repeatable-read", "title": "Transactions in PostgreSQL: READ COMMITTED vs. REPEATABLE READ", "date": "2018-11-28", "passages": ["One important aspect of transactions in PostgreSQL, and therefore in all other modern relational databases, is the ability to control when a row is visible to a user and when it is not. The ANSI SQL standard proposes 4 transaction isolation levels (READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE) to allow users to explicitly control the behavior of the database engine. Unfortunately, the existence of transaction isolation levels is still not as widely known as it should be. Therefore I decided to blog about this topic, to give more PostgreSQL users the chance to apply this very important, yet under-appreciated feature.", "The two most commonly used transaction isolation levels are READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ. In PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED is the default isolation level and should be used for normal OLTP operations. In contrast to other systems, such as DB2 or Informix, PostgreSQL does not provide support for READ UNCOMMITTED, which I personally consider to be a thing of the past anyway.\n\nIn READ COMMITTED mode, every SQL statement will see changes which have already been committed (e.g. new rows added to the database) by some other transactions. In other words: If you run the same SELECT statement multiple times within the same transaction, you might see different results. This is something you have to consider when writing an application.", "However, within a statement the data you see is constant – it does not change. A SELECT statement (or any other statement) will not see changes committed WHILE the statement is running. Within an SQL statement, data and time are basically “frozen”.\n\nIn the case of REPEATABLE READ the situation is quite different: A transaction running in REPEATABLE READ mode will never see the effects of transactions committing concurrently – it will keep seeing the same data and offer you a consistent snapshot throughout the entire transaction. If your goal is to do reporting or if you are running some kind of data warehousing workload, REPEATABLE READ is exactly what you need, because it provides consistency. All pages of your report will see exactly the same set of data. There is no need to worry about concurrent transactions."]}
</tool_result>

{"url": "https://dev.to/mohhddhassan/postgresql-backups-and-point-in-time-recovery-with-pgbackrest-13gp", "title": "PostgreSQL Backups and Point-in-Time Recovery with pgBackRest", "date": "2026-03-13", "passages": ["This article is part of a series on PostgreSQL WAL.

Part 1 - How PostgreSQL WAL Actually Works

Part 2 - How Debezium Uses PostgreSQL WAL for CDC

Part 3 - PostgreSQL Backups with pgBackRest and PITR

In the previous articles, we've explored how PostgreSQL records every change inside the database using **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)**.

We also saw how tools like Debezium can read WAL to stream database changes in real time.

But WAL has another very important role.

It enables **database backups and recovery**.

By combining a base backup with archived WAL segments, PostgreSQL can restore a database to **any specific moment in time**. This capability is known as **Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)**.

In this article, we’ll explore how this works and how to implement it using pgBackRest.", "Point-in-Time Recovery works by combining two components:

```
                              Base Backup
                                   +
                        Continuous WAL Archiving
                                   =
                         Point-in-Time Recovery
```
The recovery flow looks like this:

```
                               Base Backup
                                    │
                                    ▼
                              Restore Backup
                                    │
                                    ▼
                           Replay WAL Segments
                                    │
                                    ▼
                            Reach Target Time
```
Because WAL contains every change in chronological order, PostgreSQL can replay those changes to reconstruct the database state at any moment.", "Throughout this series, we’ve seen how **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)** forms the foundation for several critical PostgreSQL features.

The same WAL mechanism powers:

- crash recovery
- replication
- change data capture
- backups
- point-in-time recovery

Understanding WAL makes it easier to understand how PostgreSQL maintains reliability and data safety in production environments.

Tools like pgBackRest build on top of this mechanism to provide robust backup and restore workflows."]}
</tool_result>

{"url": "https://simplyblock.io/blog/point-in-time-recovery-for-postgresql-on-kubernetes", "title": "PostgreSQL PITR on Kubernetes | simplyblock", "date": "2026-03-11", "passages": ["Plenty of Kubernetes backup content treats point-in-time recovery like a fancy snapshot feature. That is not how PostgreSQL works.

PostgreSQL point-in-time recovery, or PITR, is a recovery model built from two things together:

- a physical base backup
- a continuous archive of write-ahead log, or WAL, files

The current PostgreSQL documentation is explicit about this. PITR combines a file-system-level backup with archived WAL, then replays WAL until the target time you want to restore to. In other words, snapshots can help, but snapshots alone are not PITR.

That distinction matters even more on Kubernetes, where teams often have:

- CSI snapshots
- operator-managed backups
- object-store retention
- multiple PVCs
- automation that looks reassuring until the first real restore", "If you want a design that is operationally sane, keep it simple:

- take regular physical base backups
- archive WAL continuously to object storage
- use snapshots to accelerate recovery when your storage stack supports them
- restore into a new cluster, then validate before promotion

That avoids two common traps:

- treating snapshots as the whole disaster-recovery plan
- overcomplicating recovery with too many one-off scripts and manual steps

If your operator supports it, snapshot-based recovery can shorten the time needed to rehydrate large datasets. CloudNativePG, for example, supports restoring from a `VolumeSnapshot` and then applying archived WAL to reach the target time. It also warns that if you use separate WAL storage, that snapshot must be included too.", "At minimum, you need a recoverable base backup, continuous WAL archiving, and a tested restore workflow that can recover to a specific target time or restore point."]}
</tool_result>

{"url": "https://cybertec-postgresql.com/en/transactions-in-postgresql-read-committed-vs-repeatable-read", "title": "Transactions in PostgreSQL: READ COMMITTED vs. REPEATABLE READ", "date": "2018-11-28", "passages": ["One important aspect of transactions in PostgreSQL, and therefore in all other modern relational databases, is the ability to control when a row is visible to a user and when it is not. The ANSI SQL standard proposes 4 transaction isolation levels (READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE) to allow users to explicitly control the behavior of the database engine. Unfortunately, the existence of transaction isolation levels is still not as widely known as it should be. Therefore I decided to blog about this topic, to give more PostgreSQL users the chance to apply this very important, yet under-appreciated feature.", "The two most commonly used transaction isolation levels are READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ. In PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED is the default isolation level and should be used for normal OLTP operations. In contrast to other systems, such as DB2 or Informix, PostgreSQL does not provide support for READ UNCOMMITTED, which I personally consider to be a thing of the past anyway.\n\nIn READ COMMITTED mode, every SQL statement will see changes which have already been committed (e.g. new rows added to the database) by some other transactions. In other words: If you run the same SELECT statement multiple times within the same transaction, you might see different results. This is something you have to consider when writing an application.", "However, within a statement the data you see is constant – it does not change. A SELECT statement (or any other statement) will not see changes committed WHILE the statement is running. Within an SQL statement, data and time are basically “frozen”.\n\nIn the case of REPEATABLE READ the situation is quite different: A transaction running in REPEATABLE READ mode will never see the effects of transactions committing concurrently – it will keep seeing the same data and offer you a consistent snapshot throughout the entire transaction. If your goal is to do reporting or if you are running some kind of data warehousing workload, REPEATABLE READ is exactly what you need, because it provides consistency. All pages of your report will see exactly the same set of data. There is no need to worry about concurrent transactions."]}
</tool_result>

Part 1 - How PostgreSQL WAL Actually Works

Part 2 - How Debezium Uses PostgreSQL WAL for CDC

Part 3 - PostgreSQL Backups with pgBackRest and PITR

In the previous articles, we've explored how PostgreSQL records every change inside the database using **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)**.

We also saw how tools like Debezium can read WAL to stream database changes in real time.

But WAL has another very important role.

It enables **database backups and recovery**.

By combining a base backup with archived WAL segments, PostgreSQL can restore a database to **any specific moment in time**. This capability is known as **Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)**.

In this article, we’ll explore how this works and how to implement it using pgBackRest.", "Point-in-Time Recovery works by combining two components:

```
                              Base Backup
                                   +
                        Continuous WAL Archiving
                                   =
                         Point-in-Time Recovery
```
The recovery flow looks like this:

```
                               Base Backup
                                    │
                                    ▼
                              Restore Backup
                                    │
                                    ▼
                           Replay WAL Segments
                                    │
                                    ▼
                            Reach Target Time
```
Because WAL contains every change in chronological order, PostgreSQL can replay those changes to reconstruct the database state at any moment.", "Throughout this series, we’ve seen how **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)** forms the foundation for several critical PostgreSQL features.

The same WAL mechanism powers:

- crash recovery
- replication
- change data capture
- backups
- point-in-time recovery

Understanding WAL makes it easier to understand how PostgreSQL maintains reliability and data safety in production environments.

Tools like pgBackRest build on top of this mechanism to provide robust backup and restore workflows."]}
</tool_result>

{"url": "https://simplyblock.io/blog/point-in-time-recovery-for-postgresql-on-kubernetes", "title": "PostgreSQL PITR on Kubernetes | simplyblock", "date": "2026-03-11", "passages": ["Plenty of Kubernetes backup content treats point-in-time recovery like a fancy snapshot feature. That is not how PostgreSQL works.

PostgreSQL point-in-time recovery, or PITR, is a recovery model built from two things together:

- a physical base backup
- a continuous archive of write-ahead log, or WAL, files

The current PostgreSQL documentation is explicit about this. PITR combines a file-system-level backup with archived WAL, then replays WAL until the target time you want to restore to. In other words, snapshots can help, but snapshots alone are not PITR.

That distinction matters even more on Kubernetes, where teams often have:

- CSI snapshots
- operator-managed backups
- object-store retention
- multiple PVCs
- automation that looks reassuring until the first real restore", "If you want a design that is operationally sane, keep it simple:

- take regular physical base backups
- archive WAL continuously to object storage
- use snapshots to accelerate recovery when your storage stack supports them
- restore into a new cluster, then validate before promotion

That avoids two common traps:

- treating snapshots as the whole disaster-recovery plan
- overcomplicating recovery with too many one-off scripts and manual steps

If your operator supports it, snapshot-based recovery can shorten the time needed to rehydrate large datasets. CloudNativePG, for example, supports restoring from a `VolumeSnapshot` and then applying archived WAL to reach the target time. It also warns that if you use separate WAL storage, that snapshot must be included too.", "At minimum, you need a recoverable base backup, continuous WAL archiving, and a tested restore workflow that can recover to a specific target time or restore point."]}
</tool_result>

{"url": "https://stackharbor.com/en/knowledge-base/postgres-pitr-wal-archiving", "title": "PostgreSQL Point-in-Time Recovery with WAL Archiving | Stack Harbor", "date": "2026-07-21", "passages": ["Point-in-time recovery (PITR) lets you restore a self-managed PostgreSQL cluster to any exact moment — the instant before a bad `DELETE`, not just last night’s snapshot. It rests on two pieces: a physical base backup taken with `pg_basebackup`, and a continuous stream of write-ahead log (WAL) segments shipped off the server by `archive_command`. To recover, you lay down the base backup, point `restore_command` at the WAL archive, set `recovery_target_time` to the moment you want, drop a `recovery.signal` file, and start the server. It replays WAL forward from the backup until it reaches your target, then stops. On PostgreSQL 15, 16, and 17 the old `recovery.conf` is gone — recovery settings live in `postgresql.auto.conf` and the presence of `recovery.signal` is what puts the server into recovery mode. The configuration is a few lines; the part that actually saves you is rehearsing the restore before you need it.", "```
LOG:  starting point-in-time recovery to 2026-07-21 14:19:55-04
LOG:  restored log file "000000010000000000000004" from archive
LOG:  recovery stopping before commit of transaction 1234, time 2026-07-21 14:19:56.02-04
LOG:  recovery has paused
HINT:  Execute pg_wal_replay_resume() to promote.
```
**10. Inspect, then promote.** Connect and check the data (see the next section). When satisfied, end recovery and open the cluster read-write.

`SELECT pg_wal_replay_resume();`
The server finishes on a new timeline and begins accepting writes. `pg_promote()` is the equivalent when you want to force the end immediately.", "For the authoritative reference on every parameter, see the PostgreSQL manual on Continuous Archiving and Point-in-Time Recovery and the recovery target settings.

If this is the kind of work you’d rather never own again, it’s the daily job of Managed Cloud Ops — book an infrastructure review."]}

<source id="1" title="Transactions in PostgreSQL: READ COMMITTED vs. REPEATABLE READ" site="CYBERTEC PostgreSQL | Services & Support" published="2018-11-28">
Citation label: [1]

One important aspect of transactions in PostgreSQL, and therefore in all other modern relational databases, is the ability to control when a row is visible to a user and when it is not. The ANSI SQL standard proposes 4 transaction isolation levels (READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE) to allow users to explicitly control the behavior of the database engine. Unfortunately, the existence of transaction isolation levels is still not as widely known as it should be. Therefore I decided to blog about this topic, to give more PostgreSQL users the chance to apply this very important, yet under-appreciated feature.

The two most commonly used transaction isolation levels are READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ. In PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED is the default isolation level and should be used for normal OLTP operations. In contrast to other systems, such as DB2 or Informix, PostgreSQL does not provide support for READ UNCOMMITTED, which I personally consider to be a thing of the past anyway.

In READ COMMITTED mode, every SQL statement will see changes which have already been committed (e.g. new rows added to the database) by some other transactions. In other words: If you run the same SELECT statement multiple times within the same transaction, you might see different results. This is something you have to consider when writing an application.

However, within a statement the data you see is constant – it does not change. A SELECT statement (or any other statement) will not see changes committed WHILE the statement is running. Within an SQL statement, data and time are basically “frozen”.

In the case of REPEATABLE READ the situation is quite different: A transaction running in REPEATABLE READ mode will never see the effects of transactions committing concurrently – it will keep seeing the same data and offer you a consistent snapshot throughout the entire transaction. If your goal is to do reporting or if you are running some kind of data warehousing workload, REPEATABLE READ is exactly what you need, because it provides consistency. All pages of your report will see exactly the same set of data. There is no need to worry about concurrent transactions.
</source>
<source id="2" title="PostgreSQL Backups and Point-in-Time Recovery with pgBackRest" site="DEV Community" published="2026-03-13">
Citation label: [2]

This article is part of a series on PostgreSQL WAL.

Part 1 - How PostgreSQL WAL Actually Works

Part 2 - How Debezium Uses PostgreSQL WAL for CDC

Part 3 - PostgreSQL Backups with pgBackRest and PITR

In the previous articles, we've explored how PostgreSQL records every change inside the database using **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)**.

We also saw how tools like Debezium can read WAL to stream database changes in real time.

But WAL has another very important role.

It enables **database backups and recovery**.

By combining a base backup with archived WAL segments, PostgreSQL can restore a database to **any specific moment in time**. This capability is known as **Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)**.

In this article, we’ll explore how this works and how to implement it using pgBackRest.

Section: How WAL Enables Point-in-Time Recovery
Point-in-Time Recovery works by combining two components:

```
                              Base Backup
                                   +
                        Continuous WAL Archiving
                                   =
                         Point-in-Time Recovery
```
The recovery flow looks like this:

```
                               Base Backup
                                    │
                                    ▼
                              Restore Backup
                                    │
                                    ▼
                           Replay WAL Segments
                                    │
                                    ▼
                            Reach Target Time
```
Because WAL contains every change in chronological order, PostgreSQL can replay those changes to reconstruct the database state at any moment.

Section: Final Thoughts
Throughout this series, we’ve seen how **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)** forms the foundation for several critical PostgreSQL features.

The same WAL mechanism powers:

- crash recovery
- replication
- change data capture
- backups
- point-in-time recovery

Understanding WAL makes it easier to understand how PostgreSQL maintains reliability and data safety in production environments.

Tools like pgBackRest build on top of this mechanism to provide robust backup and restore workflows.
</source>

<source id="4" title="PostgreSQL PITR on Kubernetes | simplyblock" site="Simplyblock" published="2026-03-11">
Citation label: [4]

Plenty of Kubernetes backup content treats point-in-time recovery like a fancy snapshot feature. That is not how PostgreSQL works.

PostgreSQL point-in-time recovery, or PITR, is a recovery model built from two things together:

- a physical base backup
- a continuous archive of write-ahead log, or WAL, files

The current PostgreSQL documentation is explicit about this. PITR combines a file-system-level backup with archived WAL, then replays WAL until the target time you want to restore to. In other words, snapshots can help, but snapshots alone are not PITR.

That distinction matters even more on Kubernetes, where teams often have:

- CSI snapshots
- operator-managed backups
- object-store retention
- multiple PVCs
- automation that looks reassuring until the first real restore

Section: A Practical PITR Design for Kubernetes
If you want a design that is operationally sane, keep it simple:

- take regular physical base backups
- archive WAL continuously to object storage
- use snapshots to accelerate recovery when your storage stack supports them
- restore into a new cluster, then validate before promotion

That avoids two common traps:

- treating snapshots as the whole disaster-recovery plan
- overcomplicating recovery with too many one-off scripts and manual steps

If your operator supports it, snapshot-based recovery can shorten the time needed to rehydrate large datasets. CloudNativePG, for example, supports restoring from a `VolumeSnapshot` and then applying archived WAL to reach the target time. It also warns that if you use separate WAL storage, that snapshot must be included too.

Section: What does PostgreSQL PITR on Kubernetes actually require?
At minimum, you need a recoverable base backup, continuous WAL archiving, and a tested restore workflow that can recover to a specific target time or restore point.
</source>
<source id="5" title="PostgreSQL Point-in-Time Recovery with WAL Archiving | Stack Harbor" site="Stack Harbor" published="2026-07-21">
Citation label: [5]

Point-in-time recovery (PITR) lets you restore a self-managed PostgreSQL cluster to any exact moment — the instant before a bad `DELETE`, not just last night’s snapshot. It rests on two pieces: a physical base backup taken with `pg_basebackup`, and a continuous stream of write-ahead log (WAL) segments shipped off the server by `archive_command`. To recover, you lay down the base backup, point `restore_command` at the WAL archive, set `recovery_target_time` to the moment you want, drop a `recovery.signal` file, and start the server. It replays WAL forward from the backup until it reaches your target, then stops. On PostgreSQL 15, 16, and 17 the old `recovery.conf` is gone — recovery settings live in `postgresql.auto.conf` and the presence of `recovery.signal` is what puts the server into recovery mode. The configuration is a few lines; the part that actually saves you is rehearsing the restore before you need it.

Section: Step-by-step
```
LOG:  starting point-in-time recovery to 2026-07-21 14:19:55-04
LOG:  restored log file "000000010000000000000004" from archive
LOG:  recovery stopping before commit of transaction 1234, time 2026-07-21 14:19:56.02-04
LOG:  recovery has paused
HINT:  Execute pg_wal_replay_resume() to promote.
```
**10. Inspect, then promote.** Connect and check the data (see the next section). When satisfied, end recovery and open the cluster read-write.

`SELECT pg_wal_replay_resume();`
The server finishes on a new timeline and begins accepting writes. `pg_promote()` is the equivalent when you want to force the end immediately.

Section: When this is the wrong approach
For the authoritative reference on every parameter, see the PostgreSQL manual on Continuous Archiving and Point-in-Time Recovery and the recovery target settings.

If this is the kind of work you’d rather never own again, it’s the daily job of Managed Cloud Ops — book an infrastructure review.
</source>

message.content:
When the last filename is unlinked while a process still has the file open, the file's inode remains accessible through the open file handle. The process can continue to read from and write to the file using its file descriptor, even though the file name is no longer visible in the file system [1]. This is because the file handle points to the inode, which persists until all file descriptors referencing it are closed.

A relative symbolic-link target is anchored relative to the parent directory of the symlink itself [3].

Last updated: March 18, 2024

In this tutorial, we’ll see how the system behaves when we delete, move, or replace a file that has open file handles.

First of all, we’ll briefly discuss files and inodes. Then, we’ll go through the different scenarios and see what happens in each of them.

When we work on a Linux file system, it uses inodes to store information about the files.

When we list the files in a folder, we see links to inodes. **An inode can have more than one link, and those can be symbolic or hard links**.

We can use *stat* on a file and see which inode it refers to:

```
$ stat hardlink_inode_example 
  File: hardlink_inode_example
  Size: 0               Blocks: 0          IO Block: 4096   regular empty file
Device: fd03h/64771d    Inode: 20448632    Links: 2
```
Notice that **the hard link also points to the same inode 20448632**. Both files, *hardlink_inode_example* and *inode_example*, are hard links to the same inode.

Unlike hard links, symbolic links have their own inode numbers.

With all this in mind, **we can think of a file name as an alias for an inode, and we can have more than one file linked to the same inode**.

When we open a file, we get a *file descriptor* pointing to it, also called *file handle*. We can use the opened file handle of a deleted file. We can write to and read from it as if the file exists. **The file name won’t be visible in the file system, but our file handle will point to the inode, which still exists**.

Inside the first sub-shell, we start by waiting one second. We do this to be sure the second sub-shell has started and opened the file. Then, we write two lines to the file descriptor *4*, one before removing the file and another after that. We also test that the file doesn’t exist before writing the last line. We do this just for clarity.

**The second sub-shell starts by waiting two seconds, so it keeps the file opened while the first sub-shell writes to it and removes it**. After that, it prints the content of the file handle *4*.

Let’s run it and see what happens:

```
$ ./remove_opened_file.sh 
The file /tmp/remove_example was removed.
This is the content in file handle 4:
Before rm.
After rm.
```

passages.heading: Sharing symbolic links in Rational Team Concert / Overview
passages.text:
What are symbolic links? They live amongst your files and directories on your computer’s file system but they have no contents of their own. Instead, when they are inspected they reveal the contents of a target file or directory. Whenever the contents of the target changes so too does the contents of the symlink. They are also known as soft links or symlinks.

  When a symlink is created on your computer all that is kept are the details about the target. For instance, all platforms store  the path of the target while the Windows platform stores the target type as well (file/directory). A target path can look like  `C:compiler-xyzheadersstdio.h` or `../../modulexyz/headers`. The paths must follow the conventions for file system  paths set by the platform. For example, the Windows platform uses "" separate segments in a path while Unix platforms use "/".

passages.heading: Sharing symbolic links in Rational Team Concert / Overview
passages.text: The other kind of symlink target is called "relative." Relative paths use certain anchors that are resolved relative to the  parent directory of the symlink itself. For instance, a target path `../dir2` resolves to a directory called "dir2" that  is located in the directory above where the symlink is located. If the path doesn’t have any anchors or any slash ( or /) at the  start of the path then it is relative to the parent directory where the symlink is located. E.g. `dir3/myfile.txt` targets  a file called "myfile.txt" in a directory called "dir3" that sits beside the symlink.

passages.heading: Sharing symbolic links in Rational Team Concert / Overview
passages.text:
..module2module2.h        # Windows - symlink target the module2.h header file up one directory and over in the module2 directory  ../../images/banner.gif     # Linux - symlink targets the banner.gif image file up two directories and over in the images directory  directory3util.c           # Windows - symlink targets the util.c C file of directory3. directory3 is in the same directory as the symlink  file.txt                    # Windows/Linux - symlink targets file.txt beside the symlink in the same directory  

Symlinks with a relative target tend to work well when shared with other people because they are not as susceptible to differences in the way that other people’s computers are set up. Relative links are more likely to break with more localized differences in the directory structure such as moving the symlink or a file/directory that it uses in its target.

{"url": "https://baeldung.com/linux/open-file-handle-after-move-delete", "title": "What Happens to Open File Handle if File Is Moved or Deleted | Baeldung on Linux", "date": "2021-05-30", "passages": ["Learn through the super-clean Baeldung Pro experience:

>> Membership and Baeldung Pro.

No ads, dark-mode and 6 months free of IntelliJ Idea Ultimate to start with.

Last updated: March 18, 2024

In this tutorial, we’ll see how the system behaves when we delete, move, or replace a file that has open file handles.

First of all, we’ll briefly discuss files and inodes. Then, we’ll go through the different scenarios and see what happens in each of them.

When we work on a Linux file system, it uses inodes to store information about the files.

When we list the files in a folder, we see links to inodes. **An inode can have more than one link, and those can be symbolic or hard links**.

We can use *stat* on a file and see which inode it refers to:", "```
$ stat hardlink_inode_example 
  File: hardlink_inode_example
  Size: 0               Blocks: 0          IO Block: 4096   regular empty file
Device: fd03h/64771d    Inode: 20448632    Links: 2
```
Notice that **the hard link also points to the same inode 20448632**. Both files, *hardlink_inode_example* and *inode_example*, are hard links to the same inode.

Unlike hard links, symbolic links have their own inode numbers.

With all this in mind, **we can think of a file name as an alias for an inode, and we can have more than one file linked to the same inode**.

When we open a file, we get a *file descriptor* pointing to it, also called *file handle*. We can use the opened file handle of a deleted file. We can write to and read from it as if the file exists. **The file name won’t be visible in the file system, but our file handle will point to the inode, which still exists**.", "Inside the first sub-shell, we start by waiting one second. We do this to be sure the second sub-shell has started and opened the file. Then, we write two lines to the file descriptor *4*, one before removing the file and another after that. We also test that the file doesn’t exist before writing the last line. We do this just for clarity.

**The second sub-shell starts by waiting two seconds, so it keeps the file opened while the first sub-shell writes to it and removes it**. After that, it prints the content of the file handle *4*.

Let’s run it and see what happens:

```
$ ./remove_opened_file.sh 
The file /tmp/remove_example was removed.
This is the content in file handle 4:
Before rm.
After rm.
```
As we see, **the second sub-shell prints both lines even when the file doesn’t exist**.

 This behavior is because 

The system removes the inode when:"]}

<source id="3" title="Sharing symbolic links in Rational Team Concert" site="jazz.net" published="2012-07-05">
Citation label: [3]

Section: Sharing symbolic links in Rational Team Concert / Overview
What are symbolic links? They live amongst your files and directories on your computer’s file system but they have no contents of their own. Instead, when they are inspected they reveal the contents of a target file or directory. Whenever the contents of the target changes so too does the contents of the symlink. They are also known as soft links or symlinks.

  When a symlink is created on your computer all that is kept are the details about the target. For instance, all platforms store  the path of the target while the Windows platform stores the target type as well (file/directory). A target path can look like  `C:compiler-xyzheadersstdio.h` or `../../modulexyz/headers`. The paths must follow the conventions for file system  paths set by the platform. For example, the Windows platform uses "" separate segments in a path while Unix platforms use "/".  

Section: Sharing symbolic links in Rational Team Concert / Overview
  The other kind of symlink target is called "relative." Relative paths use certain anchors that are resolved relative to the  parent directory of the symlink itself. For instance, a target path `../dir2` resolves to a directory called "dir2" that  is located in the directory above where the symlink is located. If the path doesn’t have any anchors or any slash ( or /) at the  start of the path then it is relative to the parent directory where the symlink is located. E.g. `dir3/myfile.txt` targets  a file called "myfile.txt" in a directory called "dir3" that sits beside the symlink.  

Section: Sharing symbolic links in Rational Team Concert / Overview
  ..module2module2.h        # Windows - symlink target the module2.h header file up one directory and over in the module2 directory  ../../images/banner.gif     # Linux - symlink targets the banner.gif image file up two directories and over in the images directory  directory3util.c           # Windows - symlink targets the util.c C file of directory3. directory3 is in the same directory as the symlink  file.txt                    # Windows/Linux - symlink targets file.txt beside the symlink in the same directory  

Symlinks with a relative target tend to work well when shared with other people because they are not as susceptible to differences in the way that other people’s computers are set up. Relative links are more likely to break with more localized differences in the directory structure such as moving the symlink or a file/directory that it uses in its target.

Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in August 2012 [2]. The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) launched on December 25, 2021 [1][3]. 

JWST operates in a halo orbit around the Sun–Earth L2 Lagrange point, approximately 1.5 million kilometers from Earth [1]. passages.heading: About the James Webb Space Telescope
passages.text: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is the most ambitious and powerful space observatory ever constructed. A joint project between NASA, the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Canadian Space Agency (CSA), it was launched on 25 December 2021 aboard an Ariane 5 rocket from the Guiana Space Centre in Kourou, French Guiana. After a month-long journey, JWST reached its operational position at the Sun–Earth L2 Lagrange point, approximately 1.5 million kilometres from Earth — nearly four times farther than the Moon.

passages.heading: What is Voyager 1?
passages.text:
Voyager 1 has been exploring our solar system since 1977. The probe is now in interstellar space, the region outside the heliopause, or the bubble of energetic particles and magnetic fields from the Sun. Voyager 1 was launched after Voyager 2, but because of a faster route it exited the asteroid belt earlier than its twin, and it overtook Voyager 2 on Dec. 15, 1977.

- Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring around Jupiter and two new Jovian moons: Thebe and Metis.
- At Saturn, Voyager 1 found five new moons and a new ring called the G-ring.
- Voyager 1 was the first spacecraft to cross the heliosphere, the boundary where the influences from outside our solar system are stronger than those from our Sun.
- Voyager 1 is the first human-made object to venture into interstellar space.

passages.heading: NASA Shuts Off Instrument on Voyager 1 to Keep Spacecraft Operating
passages.text:
On April 17, engineers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California shut down an instrument aboard Voyager 1, to save power and keep humanity’s first interstellar explorer going. Voyager 1 still has two science instruments operating, nearly 50 years into its mission; years ago Voyager scientists and engineers agreed on the order to shut off parts of the spacecraft, to preserve power while ensuring the mission can continue to conduct its unique science.

Read the Latest on Voyager 1

sources.title: What Is the James Webb Space Telescope?

passages.heading: It is very, very big.
passages.text: The Webb telescope is as tall as a 3-story building and as long as a tennis court! It is so big that it has to fold origami-style to fit inside the rocket to launch. The telescope will unfold, sunshield first, once in space.

passages.heading: It can see through dust clouds.
passages.text: The James Webb Space Telescope sees the universe in light that is invisible to human eyes. This light is called **infrared radiation**, and we can feel it as heat. Firefighters use infrared cameras to see and rescue people through the smoke in a fire. The James Webb Space Telescope will use its infrared cameras to see through dust in our universe. Stars and planets form inside those dust clouds, so peeking inside could lead to exciting new discoveries! It will also be able to see objects (like the first galaxies) that are so far away that the expansion of the universe has made their light shift from visible to infrared!

passages.heading: What is the James Webb Space Telescope doing right now?
passages.text: The James Webb Space Telescope launched on December 25, 2021. Want to stay up to date and learn more about NASA’s biggest and most powerful telescope? The probe is now in interstellar space, the region outside the heliopause, or the bubble of energetic particles and magnetic fields from the Sun. Voyager 1 was launched after Voyager 2, but because of a faster route it exited the asteroid belt earlier than its twin, and it overtook Voyager 2 on Dec. 15, 1977.

- Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring around Jupiter and two new Jovian moons: Thebe and Metis.
- At Saturn, Voyager 1 found five new moons and a new ring called the G-ring.
- Voyager 1 was the first spacecraft to cross the heliosphere, the boundary where the influences from outside our solar system are stronger than those from our Sun.
- Voyager 1 is the first human-made object to venture into interstellar space.", "On April 17, engineers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California shut down an instrument aboard Voyager 1, to save power and keep humanity’s first interstellar explorer going. Voyager 1 still has two science instruments operating, nearly 50 years into its mission; years ago Voyager scientists and engineers agreed on the order to shut off parts of the spacecraft, to preserve power while ensuring the mission can continue to conduct its unique science.

| **Launch Site** | Cape Canaveral, Florida / Launch Complex 41 |
